events.title: Rust 1.0 released
events.summary: The Rust core team shipped Rust 1.0 on May 15, 2015 — a systems language with ownership-based memory safety.
events.about: Rust gives C/C++ performance without garbage collection — the borrow checker prevents use-after-free and data races at compile time. Used in Firefox's Servo engine, Linux kernel modules, Cloudflare, Discord, and WASM runtimes. Teams pick Rust when safety and speed both matter and GC is unacceptable.

narrative.whyChosen: Rust 1.0 promised stability after years of public iteration — a new option for memory-safe systems code.
narrative.whyImportant: Ownership and borrowing influenced how the industry thinks about safe concurrency without a runtime.
narrative.problemSolved: Systems programmers faced a false choice between C++ speed with manual memory bugs and GC languages with runtime cost.

events.title: Cargo 1.0 released
events.summary: Cargo 1.0 shipped with Rust 1.0 on May 15, 2015 — the official package manager and build tool for the Rust ecosystem.
events.about: Cargo builds projects, resolves dependencies from crates.io, and publishes semver-versioned crates — `cargo new`, `cargo build`, `cargo test`, and `cargo publish` are the Rust workflow. Lockfiles ensure reproducible builds. Example: add `serde = "1.0"` to `Cargo.toml` and Cargo fetches compatible releases automatically.

narrative.whyChosen: Stable Cargo arrived with Rust 1.0, making the language production-ready end-to-end.
narrative.whyImportant: It gave Rust a first-class package ecosystem modeled on npm and Bundler but with stronger build integration.
narrative.problemSolved: Rust needed a unified tool for dependencies, builds, tests, and publishing — not ad-hoc makefiles.

events.title: HTTP/2 standardized
events.summary: RFC 7540 published HTTP/2 on May 14, 2015 — multiplexed requests, header compression, and server push over a single TCP connection.
events.about: HTTP/2 evolved from Google's SPDY protocol — browsers and CDNs adopted it to cut page load latency. Multiple requests share one connection without head-of-line blocking at the HTTP layer; HPACK compresses headers. gRPC and many APIs run over HTTP/2 today. Example: a page loading dozens of assets in parallel on one TLS connection to the origin.

narrative.whyChosen: HTTP/2 was the first major HTTP revision since 1.1 and addressed real-world web performance bottlenecks.
narrative.whyImportant: It made multiplexing and header compression standard, paving the way for HTTP/3 over QUIC.
narrative.problemSolved: HTTP/1.1's one-request-per-connection model caused latency and inefficient use of modern networks.

events.title: JWT standardized
events.summary: RFC 7519 defined JSON Web Tokens in May 2015 — a compact, URL-safe format for signed claims between services.
events.about: JWTs encode JSON claims in a three-part base64 string: header, payload, signature. APIs issue them after login; clients send `Authorization: Bearer <token>` on later requests. Used with OAuth 2.0, OpenID Connect, and microservice auth — though teams must validate signatures, expiry, and audience carefully.

narrative.whyChosen: JWT became the default wire format for stateless API authentication after OAuth took off.
narrative.whyImportant: It standardized how services pass identity and permissions without server-side sessions.
narrative.problemSolved: Every API invented its own opaque token format; clients and gateways needed a portable standard.

sources.title: jwt.io — Introduction to JSON Web Tokens (overview)

events.title: Rollup first released
events.summary: Rich Harris published Rollup 0.3.0 on May 21, 2015 — the first meaningful public ES module bundler release with tree-shaking (earlier 0.1.x tags were experiments).
events.about: Rollup analyzes static `import`/`export` graphs and eliminates dead code — producing smaller bundles than Browserify or early webpack for library authors. It powers Vue, React tooling, and many npm packages shipped as ES modules. Example: importing one function from lodash-es ships only that function, not the entire library.

narrative.whyChosen: Rollup pioneered tree-shaking for ES modules at a time when webpack optimized CommonJS bundles.
narrative.whyImportant: It influenced webpack 2+ and proved ES module semantics enable smaller production builds.
narrative.problemSolved: Bundlers shipped entire dependency trees even when apps used a fraction of each library.

events.title: Shopify IPO
events.summary: Shopify went public on the NYSE on May 21, 2015 — raising $131 million and trading under ticker SHOP.
events.about: The IPO validated hosted e-commerce as a massive market — Shopify had grown from a snowboard shop side project to a platform powering hundreds of thousands of merchants. Public capital funded payments, POS, and fulfillment products that extended beyond online storefronts.

narrative.whyChosen: Shopify's IPO marked hosted e-commerce as a mainstream public-market category.
narrative.whyImportant: It funded expansion into payments and omnichannel retail infrastructure.
narrative.problemSolved: Merchants needed a scalable platform backed by public capital, not just venture funding.

sources.title: Shopify News — Shopify files for IPO (May 21, 2015)

events.title: Gatsby open sourced
events.summary: Kyle Mathews open sourced Gatsby on May 21, 2015 — a React-based static site generator with GraphQL data layer.
events.about: Gatsby pre-renders React pages at build time and pulls data via GraphQL from Markdown, CMSs, and APIs — blazing fast sites with component ergonomics. It powered the Jamstack movement alongside Netlify before Next.js static generation absorbed much of the market.

narrative.whyChosen: Gatsby made React static sites production-ready with a unified data layer.
narrative.whyImportant: It proved static generation and React components could coexist at scale.
narrative.problemSolved: React SPAs were slow to load; teams needed SSR/SSG without abandoning components.
